name: Zainab
definition: Zainab is a composite portrait of a Muslim woman in Navalgund taluk, Dharwad district, who rolls beedis at home while managing household responsibilities and navigating the schooling aspirations of her children. She represents the experience of women balancing piecework income with family care in a town where Urdu medium schools serve the community but higher education requires difficult choices.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Zainab wakes before dawn for namaaz and begins her day rolling beedis at the small table in her two-room house near the Navalgund bus stand. She collects tobacco and tendu leaves from a contractor each Monday and returns filled bundles by Saturday, earning about forty to fifty rupees per thousand beedis, which translates to three to four thousand rupees in a good month when her fingers and eyes cooperate. The work is tedious and her thumbs ache by evening, but it allows her to stay home with her youngest child and contribute to household expenses. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on the Navalgund-Hubballi route, bringing in six to eight thousand rupees a month depending on diesel prices and passenger flow. Together they manage rent of two thousand five hundred, ration rice under Anna Bhagya, and careful spending on vegetables, kerosene and clothes. Zainab buys from the Thursday haat and saves on gas by cooking on a chulha when time permits. The joint income barely covers expenses, and any medical cost or school fee throws the month into arrears with the neighbourhood kirana shop.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Zainab lives with her husband, three children and her mother-in-law in a rented house in the Urdu-speaking mohalla of Navalgund. Her eldest daughter is fifteen and studies in Class 10 at the government Urdu medium high school, her son is twelve and in Class 7, and her youngest daughter is six and attending the anganwadi. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, was widowed young and worked as a domestic helper for decades; she now suffers from joint pain and helps with cooking and childcare when she can. Zainab was married at seventeen, shortly after her own schooling ended in Class 8 when her family could not afford the fees and uniform for high school. Her husband is a steady man but the auto earnings are unpredictable, and he worries about competition from app-based cabs in Hubballi. Zainab makes most day-to-day decisions about food and children's needs, though larger expenses and schooling choices are discussed together. She hopes her daughters will study further than she did, but fears the cost and distance if they must go to Hubballi for PU college.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Zainab's eldest daughter attends the government Urdu medium high school in Navalgund, where she studies in Class 10 and prepares for her SSLC exams. The school is a ten-minute walk from home and there are no fees, though Zainab spends about fifteen hundred rupees a year on notebooks, pens, and the occasional tuition class for mathematics. Her daughter is a serious student and Zainab dreams of her becoming a teacher, but after SSLC the family will face a hard choice: Navalgund has only one PU college and it teaches in Kannada medium, which her daughter struggles with, while the Urdu-medium colleges are in Hubballi, requiring daily bus fare or hostel costs they cannot afford. The youngest girl goes to the anganwadi and will start Class 1 next year. Zainab attended school herself until Class 8 in a village near Gadag, learning to read Urdu and some Kannada, and she insists her children continue as long as possible. The free Shakti bus pass helps her daughter travel for exams or errands, and the midday meal keeps them in school, but Zainab knows that after SSLC the real costs and distances begin.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Zainab's mother-in-law has chronic knee pain and occasional breathlessness, visiting the government hospital in Navalgund for check-ups and tablets that sometimes run out before the next appointment. Zainab herself suffers from recurrent back pain from long hours hunched over the beedi work and poor eyesight that makes rolling harder each year; she has never had glasses fitted. Her youngest daughter was anaemic as a toddler, and the anganwadi worker advised eggs and greens, but eggs are costly and the family eats them only occasionally. When someone falls seriously ill they go to Hubballi, to KIMS or a private clinic, and the costs can run into thousands; two years ago her husband's accident required stitches and an X-ray that cost four thousand rupees, borrowed from relatives and still being repaid. The family is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat but navigating the hospital cashless process is confusing, and they often pay upfront and fail to claim reimbursement. Zainab boils neem leaves for fevers and uses home remedies her mother-in-law teaches her. She worries about her own health as she ages, knowing there is no pension or insurance if she cannot work, and that her daughters will have to bear the burden.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Zainab's family are Sunni Muslims and the rhythm of her week follows namaaz times, Friday visits to the masjid for her husband, and Ramzan fasting and Eid preparations that bring the mohalla together. The Urdu-speaking community in Navalgund is close-knit; neighbours lend small sums, share news of work or school admissions, and gather for weddings and condolence visits. Zainab's mother-in-law recalls the annual urus at Shishunala Sharif in nearby Shiggaon, where both Hindus and Muslims visit the dargah, and Zainab took her children there once. She values the respect the dargah commands across communities and wishes more people remembered that shared devotion. The Urdu medium school and madrasa are anchors of community life, though Zainab notes that some better-off families now send children to Kannada or English medium schools in Hubballi. She feels the double edge of being Muslim in a time of uncertain politics: proud of her faith and community solidarity, but wary of her children facing bias or being left behind if Urdu medium limits their opportunities. Her mother-in-law insists on modest dress and Quranic learning; Zainab herself wears a headscarf and prays daily, finding comfort in faith even when money is short.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Zainab's family has a ration card and receives Anna Bhagya rice each month, a staple she depends on. She receives Gruha Lakshmi payments, but the last two instalments were delayed and arrived together in August 2026, causing confusion about the schedule. Her daughter uses the Shakti free bus pass to travel to Hubballi for tuition once a fortnight, and Zainab sees it as a great help though the NWKRTC buses from Navalgund are often crowded. The family has not received direct crop compensation because they own no land, but the drought of 2023 and again in 2026 raised vegetable prices and hit the auto business as rural passengers made fewer trips. Zainab knows little about the Mahadayi water project or Almatti dam issues that dominate the newspapers her husband brings home, but she understands that Navalgund farmers are angry about delayed canal water and that this anger flows into every election. The winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha is a pride for North Karnataka, her husband says, but she wonders what it delivers for people like them. She has never visited a taluk office or dealt with Bhoomi or Seva Sindhu; her husband handles such matters. She trusts the anganwadi worker, who is kind and from the same mohalla, more than distant bureaucrats.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Zainab worries most about her children's future: whether her eldest daughter can continue to PU college and become a teacher, whether her son will stay in school or drift into unskilled work, and whether her youngest will have better chances than she did. She is proud that her daughter studies seriously and knows Urdu, Kannada and some English, but fears the Urdu medium will close doors in a job market that prizes Kannada or English. The delays in Gruha Lakshmi frustrate her because every month's budget is tight, and she resents hearing about corruption when basic services falter. She wishes Navalgund had better hospitals, an Urdu-medium PU college, and more beedi contractors so women could earn without travelling. Zainab admires the discipline of her mother-in-law's generation but sees the world changing fast: her daughter speaks of becoming independent, of work and choice, ideas that make Zainab both hopeful and anxious. She is proud of her faith and her community's resilience, and she wants outsiders to see Muslim families like hers as hardworking and rooted in Karnataka's soil, not as outsiders or threats. She dreams her children will not have to roll beedis or drive autos, that education will lift them, but every year the costs and distances remind her how hard that dream is to reach.
